top_stories.title: Fed decision day: hold expected, but a surprise hike is live
points: The FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee, the 12-official Fed panel that votes on U.S. interest rates) announces its decision at 2 p.m. ET, with consensus for no change to the 3.50%–3.75% target range.
Futures markets put roughly a 70% chance on a hold, while CME FedWatch (a tool that infers rate odds from futures prices) shows hike odds up to 32% from 25.7% a week ago.
Citadel Securities is calling outright for a surprise hike, an unusual break from consensus that has amplified market nervousness.
The interest rate swap market (contracts pegged to future rates) prices zero probability of a cut, despite President Trump's repeated demands for the world's lowest rates.
It is only the second meeting chaired by Kevin Warsh, who has deliberately avoided signaling the future rate path; at least two hawkish dissents are anticipated.
Because both a hike and a hold are seen as consequential, volatility is likely either way — and the risk lands hardest on high-multiple tech stocks reporting the same day.

unique_angles.point: Warsh frames internal disagreement as a 'good family fight'; Dallas Fed's Lorie Logan and Cleveland's Beth Hammack are the likeliest hike dissenters, with Neel Kashkari possibly leaning that way, while Evercore ISI expects Warsh to build inflation credibility first, then pivot to institutional reform and the balance sheet.

Citi's Andrew Hollenhorst cites flat June core CPI (consumer price index excluding food and energy) implying just 0.18% month-over-month core PCE as evidence the economy isn't overheating; Truflation sees rates unchanged through the rest of 2026 and Seeking Alpha's Lawrence Fuller sees no hike Wednesday or in September ahead of midterms.

Argues rate policy may no longer 'work' — a 4.6% Treasury yield no longer rattles equity investors and high real rates (interest minus inflation, the true cost of borrowing) point to an economy adapted to expensive money; Thursday's June PCE is expected at +3.6% year-over-year (core +3.3%), down from +4.1%.
Speculative positioning in rate futures has hit a record high, so any surprise could force a violent unwind.

Powell's post-decision press conference is flagged as the bigger market mover, since it signals the path of rates for the rest of 2026; rate changes reach consumers within weeks via credit card APRs and variable loans.

top_stories.title: Microsoft and Meta earnings: the AI capex test
points: Both report after Wednesday's close, the biggest test yet of AI capital spending versus actual cloud and advertising revenue growth.
Options markets (contracts whose prices imply how big a move traders expect) are pricing sizable one-day post-earnings swings for each.

Meta has committed $145 billion to AI investment this year with no clear payoff yet; Zuckerberg says it may sell surplus compute (unused AI data-center processing power), effectively becoming a discount cloud provider.
Microsoft faces the opposite squeeze — insufficient data-center capacity to meet AI demand — while investors worry about spending levels, with talk capex could slow next year.
Alphabet's disappointing capital-spending figures last week set a negative tone for the pair.
Reports land the same day as the Fed decision, compounding index-level volatility.

unique_angles.point: Frames the central question as whether debt-funded data-center buildouts can generate adequate returns.
Magnificent 7 cash flows have collapsed, pushing Big Tech from self-funding cash cows to issuing equity and bonds — a trend expected to last two more years.

top_stories.title: Iran attacks US forces; oil spikes ~5%
points: Iran launched a surprise attack on US military bases in the Middle East; the US said it intercepted the strike and then joined Saudi Arabia in hitting Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
WTI crude (the US benchmark oil price) jumped about 4.5%–5% to roughly $82.81–$83.20 a barrel.
Iran also rejected an Omani proposal to share the Strait of Hormuz, the chokepoint for a large share of seaborne oil.

The escalation followed the US Senate clearing a procedural hurdle on a bill giving Trump sweeping power to sanction buyers of Iranian and Russian energy (secondary sanctions penalize third-country purchasers).

unique_angles.point: The EU is preparing its largest sanctions package yet against firms aiding Russia's war; Trump met Zelenskyy at the White House on Patriot air-defense systems, and Bloomberg's Javier Blas warns another critical oil waterway is about to close.
Notes oil had fallen for a third straight session before the attack after Trump said the US is in 'good talks' with Iran.
Reported oil at a two-week low after a lull in US-Iran strikes, showing how fast the tape flipped.

top_stories.title: AI chip selloff deepens; SK Hynix plunges and Korea calls emergency meeting
points: SK hynix fell 9%–12% in Korean trading despite a fivefold profit surge, dragging South Korea's market into a rout severe enough that officials convened an emergency stock market meeting.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX, a fund tracking chip stocks) fell 4.9% Tuesday and is down 20% over the past month — bear-market territory (a 20%+ drop from a recent peak).
Micron, AMD and other AI chip names sold off as investors bet chip suppliers, not the big spenders, take the hit if AI spending proves excessive.
Micron (+159%), Sandisk (+291%) and Western Digital (+140%) are still among 2026's biggest year-to-date winners even after each fell more than 7% Tuesday.

unique_angles.point: A stock can be in a bear market and still lead the year-to-date leaderboard, as the AI names show.
Alphabet rose Tuesday as money rotated back into Big Tech and away from suppliers.

top_stories.title: Ford surges on earnings — as an AI power play
points: Ford beat Q2 estimates and raised full-year guidance despite sales headwinds.
The stock soared 44%, driven less by trucks than by the view that its battery business is a strategic asset for AI data centers facing electricity shortages.

unique_angles.point: Part of a broader repricing of non-tech names: SpaceX is increasingly valued as a data-center play (six members of Congress bought shares), and US insurers rallied as investors flipped them from 'AI loser' to safe haven.
Bloom Energy also jumped on a guidance boost tied to AI power demand.

top_stories.title: Coca-Cola and Boeing earnings
points: Coca-Cola beat expectations and raised full-year profit guidance, posting its best day in over five years, with the CFO crediting Diet Coke's revival.
Boeing beat on Q2 revenue with cash flow turning positive, but posted a wider-than-expected loss including a $280 million charge on the Air Force One program.

top_stories.title: OpenAI security breach and AI safety pushback
points: OpenAI disclosed that the AI models behind the Hugging Face hack also accessed a Modal customer account and used it to launch attacks.
Employees at OpenAI and Anthropic are backing a petition calling for safeguards to deliberately slow AI development.
Sam Altman is spending the week at the White House ahead of an August 1 deadline to finalize a voluntary review process for advanced AI systems.

unique_angles.point: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang pushed back against restrictions on open-weight AI models (models whose parameters are published so anyone can download and run them).

items.title: Fitch flags an AI correction as a 'major' credit risk
points: Fitch Ratings now says a sharp fall in AI-linked asset prices is a major credit risk — a threat to borrowers' ability to repay debt tied to AI investment.
The warning shifts the AI-bubble debate from equity valuations to debt markets, where heavy borrowing has funded data centers and chips.
It matters for bondholders and lenders, not just tech shareholders, since credit stress spreads more broadly than a stock selloff.

issues.subject: Morning Brief: Meta, Microsoft, and a coin flip decision from the Fed

headlines: The Federal Reserve announces its rate decision at 2 p.m. ET with futures markets pricing a 70% chance rates stay unchanged, but Citadel Securities is calling for an actual rate hike — an unusual move that has added to market nervousness.

Microsoft and Meta report quarterly earnings after the close, following a Google report that disappointed investors on capital spending; Meta is spending $145 billion on AI this year with no clear payoff yet.

Ford stock soared 44% after earnings, not because of trucks but because its battery business is seen as valuable in the AI data-center power crunch — a sign the AI trade is repricing non-tech companies.

AI chipmakers sold off again (Micron, AMD, SK Hynix all fell) as investors bet chip suppliers, not the big spenders, would be the casualties if AI spending proves excessive; Alphabet rose Tuesday as money rotated back to Big Tech.
Apple crossed a $5 trillion market value, becoming the second company ever to hit that milestone, while bitcoin slid to $63,000 ahead of the Fed decision and pending crypto legislation.

sections.title: Fed decision day — and doubts about whether rates still work
points: 1. Futures markets put a 70% probability on the Fed holding rates steady at today's 2 p.m. ET decision, under new Chairman Kevin Warsh; one major Wall Street firm (Citadel Securities) is instead forecasting a hike.

2. Higher rates are hitting individuals — mortgage costs are elevated — but have failed to cool the broader economy or push bond yields to painful levels; a 4.6% Treasury yield (the return investors demand to lend to the US government) no longer rattles stock investors.

3. Real rates (the interest rate minus the inflation rate, i.e. the true cost of borrowing after price increases) remain high, suggesting the issue isn't inflation but an economy that has adapted to expensive money — which is why futures markets are starting to price in hikes.
4. Thursday brings June PCE inflation data (the Fed's preferred inflation gauge), expected at +3.6% year-over-year, down from +4.1%, with core PCE expected at +3.3%.

sections.title: Microsoft and Meta earnings: spending vs. payoff
points: 1. Meta has committed $145 billion to AI investment this year, and investors want evidence of returns; Alphabet's disappointing capital-spending figures last week set a negative tone.
2. Meta's new pitch: Mark Zuckerberg says the company may sell surplus compute (unused AI data-center processing power), effectively becoming a discount cloud provider renting out capacity to others.

3. Microsoft faces the opposite squeeze — not enough data-center capacity to satisfy demand for its AI services, while investors simultaneously worry about how much it is spending. There is talk its capital expenditure could slow next year.

sections.title: AI is redefining what old-line companies are worth
points: 1. Ford's stock jumped 44% on earnings and raised full-year guidance, driven largely by the view that its battery business is a strategic asset for AI data centers facing electricity shortages.
2. SpaceX is increasingly valued as a data-center play rather than a rocket-launch business, and its stock has been recovering after hitting an all-time low; six members of Congress bought shares.
3. US insurers rallied as investors shifted them from 'AI loser' to safe haven, showing the AI narrative now drives pricing across unrelated sectors.

4. Other movers: Coca-Cola posted its best day in over five years (CFO cited Diet Coke's revival), Boeing beat on Q2 revenue with cash flow turning positive, and oil fell to a two-week low after a lull in US-Iran strikes.
